A few years ago I went over to another site that I won't name, and asked a question on one of their forums about. A diagnosis was made, and it was suggested that I was "skinnyfat". One of the people there, instead of the commonsense advice to cut calories and lose weight, suggested that I do a "clean bulk". Now, I researched a little about this, but I literally could not find anything beneficial to doing "bulking" and "cutting" outside of weight based sports and bodybuilding/modeling/"aesthetics" stuff. But it seems to be one of the major topics everyone talks about when discussing fitness related nutrition. Do you think there are good reasons for it?
Is there a point to "bulking" and "cutting" outside of sports with weight classes?

Fitness, especially online "groups", tend to be bent far into the narcissistic category. That means they want to look like whatever the current fad is, and for guys who want the current fad of well defined bulk, you have to go about it by doing endless bulk/cut cycles.

There's no benefit beyond appearance.

BTW, 80% of "fitness" is the diet. You absolutely need to work with weights and get in cardio, but spend the majority of your efforts on getting your diet sorted.

There's no benefit beyond appearance [and how long it takes to achieve].

+1. Cutting, in particular, is entirely about fat loss and IMO isn't fitness related. I say this as someone presently on a cut.

My guess is, if you got the label 'skinnyfat', your BMI is probably on the lower side, 17-22. If this is the case, I think the argument is that rather than keeping your calorie intake fixed and exercising (causing a net deficit) you could afford to add in resistance training and increase your caloric intake so that you are either maintaining weight or gaining slowly (300cal surplus).

If your goal were to train up -- for instance to be able to swim a 1.5K -- going for a surplus would help you to build muscle (and thus hit your goal) faster. You would likely feel less sore or worn out than you would if you maintained a deficit.

If you don't care about weight class sports, or your performance relative to your body weight then no. But then why would you even care about your fitness to begin with? It goes beyond strictly aesthetics or trends. I don't understand what you think is left as far as fitness goals if you're cutting out muscle mass and body fat ratios from the equation. They play a factor in every realistic form and consideration of fitness.

Do you think there are good reasons for it?

Sure if you want to be a big muscled person. It all depends on your goals. You seem to just want to be skinnier so just cut the calories.

Bulking/cutting is a shortcut to muscle gain and fat loss. It uses both extremes of overeating and undereating to achieve those goals rapidly. For most people, a clean diet somewhere around maintenance and 3-4 days per week of exercise is enough to achieve the goal of looking/feeling good while cutting body fat. Slow bulk or slow cut and tapered versions of those extremes that still achieve your goals of muscle gain (slow bulk) or fat loss (slow cut) although with much fewer restrictions and usually better mental health.

Even A Small Meal For A Doctor Can Tip The Balance For A Brand-Name Drug

Notice the picture of a Crestor bottle? It's a brand name statin that is commonly prescribed over generic statins. Wanna know why? Because it's more effective. Wanna know how doctors find this out? Drug rep lunches.

I've been to a number of drug rep provided lunches, and in all of them, they both showed and defended why their drugs were superior, using science and statistics. One rep for an diabetic med manufacturer showed us that while their drugs aren't actually more effective than others, they provide additional services to the patient (like an emergency hotline and a place to discuss how to take the drug properly). These doctors are probably prescribing these drugs more not because they got paid, but because they had more opportunities to learn why these drugs were superior.
